title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The shared‑initial paired design produced 300 shared initial candidates and permitted at most one repair call per failed candidate. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d. Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.9967), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.00333; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered target effect (0.10, ≈80% power) was not supported: a ceiling baseline success rate and a single repair invocation made the preregistered detectable effect unattainable. We explain these arithmetic and execution facts, record where the single repair provider trace and discordant episode are archived, disclose which preregistered secondary estimands were not produced, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for future confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Prior work shows LLMs can draft device configurations but frequently introduce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; guarded pipelines that combine generation with deterministic verification and targeted repair have been proposed to reduce misconfiguration risk. The community, however, lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that pair explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration suitable for confirmatory inference. To address this gap we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1. The sealed research question (preregistered) was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does a GVR pipeline materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and reviews document growing interest in LLMs for network management and highlight core challenges—hallucination, prompt injection, and the need for verification—that bear on operational deployment [https://openalex.org/W4406137434, https://openalex.org/W4415071524, https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical work demonstrates that LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193, 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Generate–validate–repair (GVR) and tool‑assisted prompting approaches can improve final correctness in prototypes, yet demonstrations are dataset‑specific and limited in scale [https://openalex.org/W4404652946]. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompts further motivate guarded architectures and deterministic validators for operational NetOps workflows [https://openalex.org/W4405181600, https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our work contributes a sealed, archived proof‑of‑concept benchmark and a confirmatory paired run that ties a deterministic validator to an automated repair trigger under a tightly specified retry and budget policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary hypothesis H1 asserted that the GVR pipeline would yield a higher per‑task validator pass rate than the frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration fixed task generation, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness treatment, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and a conservative repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate). All design choices and the full preregistration are archived.

Task bank and validator. A deterministic generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, difficulty label, and a required_sequence that the deterministic validator enforces. The chosen validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) is a stateless snapshot checker implementing full_intent_constraint_validation: it parses candidate commands into canonical field operations, enforces required_sequence and workflow_policies, computes the implied final_state, and returns a binary pass/fail with diagnostic violation codes and a validator trace. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after traces, and validator.valid booleans.

Paired shared‑initial design and repair policy. To isolate repair value we used a shared‑initial generation: for each task a single initial candidate was produced and used as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline’s initial candidate. The guarded condition validated that candidate and, on validator failure, could issue up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This restriction (one repair only, shared initial) was preregistered and archived; it intentionally forces any guarded benefit to arise solely from repair rather than from independent re‑sampling.

Model configuration and execution determinism. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version/requested_model = "gpt-5-mini") executed via the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with provider = "openai_responses". The model_configuration artifact records invocation settings (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The authoritative hosted provider traces are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d); reproducing identical hosted outputs requires replaying those traces or access to the same hosted model release and invocation semantics recorded in the model_configuration artifact.

Analysis plan and preregistered executors. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on the N=300 paired binary outcomes. The inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Pre‑specified missingness/sensitivity treatments and a single pre‑specified primary hypothesis were preregistered and implemented by the registered executor paired_binary_analysis_v1. The archived analysis/results.json documents produced outputs and empty secondary_results (see Results).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and repair indexing. The run completed: started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T12:41:43.384097+00:00; completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T13:07:38.995000+00:00; planned_episode_count = 600; completed_episode_count = 600; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}, confirming a single repair invocation across all tasks. The authoritative container of hosted provider call records is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). The single repair provider trace is the unique provider‑call record in that container whose stage field equals "repair"; auditors can deterministically locate it by scanning execution/raw_results.jsonl for stage=="repair" or by consulting the execution manifest cross‑references (execution/execution_manifest.json).

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. All analysis artifacts referenced above are archived in the evidence bundle.

Interpretation of discordance and inferential metrics. The exact McNemar test depends only on discordant pairs (n10 and n01). With n10=1 and n01=0 the two‑sided exact p reported by the preregistered executor is 1.0; this reflects the tiny number of discordant outcomes rather than an analytical error. Practically, the paired bootstrap CI (reported above) is a more informative summary of uncertainty under these margins because it conveys the small absolute range of possible paired differences given the observed data.

Preregistered secondary estimands. The preregistration listed secondary estimands (e.g., per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, and effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions). The archived analysis/results.json shows an empty secondary_results array; consequently no archived secondary estimand outputs were produced. This omission is recorded in the analysis artifacts and is reported here. The practical cause is the near‑ceiling baseline rates and the absence of substantive discordance: with baseline ≈0.997 there was insufficient variation to produce meaningful secondary effect‑size estimates under the preregistered estimand computations.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory hypothesis was not supported. The preregistered target was to detect an absolute paired gain of 0.10 with ≈80% power at N=300. Observed margins violate the design assumptions: because the shared initial generator already satisfied the deterministic validator in 299/300 cases, the maximum possible paired improvement (if every baseline failure were corrected) is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 — far below the preregistered target of 0.10. The arithmetic ceiling imposed by near‑perfect baseline performance combined with the constrained repair budget (one repair total occurred) makes the preregistered detectable effect unattainable in this execution.

Operational implications. The sealed result quantifies an operational regime: when a deterministic sampling semantics and a fixed generator produce near‑ceiling correctness under the chosen validator, a tightly budgeted localized repair mechanism yields negligible marginal benefit. Conversely, in lower‑quality generator regimes, adversarial or higher‑difficulty task banks, or with expanded/iterative repair budgets, GVR pipelines are more likely to yield measurable operational value. The artifacts we release enable others to implement the harder settings by: (A) increasing task difficulty or injecting adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates, (B) permitting multiple repair attempts or iterative repairs, (C) allowing multiple independent initial generations per task (selection/reranking strategies), and (D) using stateful/emulation validators to expose temporal side‑effects.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls for generator variance but does not evaluate multi‑sample baselines or selection strategies; repair rarely engaged limiting internal contrasts. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but omits vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and temporal execution dynamics. External validity: tasks are synthetic and abstracted across multi‑vendor models; only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator version (v5.0) were evaluated. Conclusion validity: the very small number of discordant outcomes (n10=1) leaves exploratory subgroup and failure‑mode inference underpowered.

Reproducibility note. The authoritative artifacts necessary to reproduce and audit the run are archived: execution/raw_results.jsonl (provider call traces; SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...), execution/model_configuration.json (requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; SHA‑256 = a40e96e2...), preregistration (SHA‑256 = a05938da...), execution/execution_manifest.json (full hash manifest cross‑references), and provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e...). The single repair provider trace is the unique provider call with stage=="repair" in execution/raw_results.jsonl and can be programmatically extracted; the execution manifest provides cross‑references for deterministic lookup.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and performed a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported; this null result follows from a ceiling baseline and minimal repair engagement (single repair invocation). We release all artifacts to enable future runs that increase task difficulty, expand repair budgets, allow multi‑generation baselines, or evaluate other models to determine the operational conditions under which GVR yields measurable improvements.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
